transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-06
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Zoe Chen (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Cobalt CTO), Maya Singh (Cobalt ML Eng), Liam Carter (Cobalt Infra), Sofia Rueda (Cobalt Product)

Auto Summary (auto gen, may be rough): quick catalog demo, focused on open models for note summarization; showed compat matrix and bench highlights; customer asked about VPC/private deploy and latency vs cost tradeoffs; next steps = bench template + POC scoping.

00:00:05 Maya Patel: All right everyone thanks for carving out time, I'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account. Today Jordan and Zoe will walk through the model catalog, show how we pick open models and read bench results. Evan, thanks for rounding up your team.
00:00:18 Evan Brooks: Yeah thanks, excited to see how fast we can get some realistic numbers. We have a shortlist but unsure about the hosting tradeoffs.
00:00:26 Jordan Li: Cool. Quick agenda: catalog filters -> pick candidate models -> read bench signals (latency / tokens / quality) -> compatibility matrix and runtime mapping -> deployment Qs. We'll stop for questions after each section.
00:00:40 Zoe Chen: small note, i'll flag how quantization profiles might shift perf numbers, especially for the 7B-13B class.
00:00:48 Maya Singh: that's useful, our samples are often 800-1,200 tokens per request, mostly clinical text with some structured fields. Latency at 1 to 1.2s is ideal, anything above 2s might be too slow for clinicians.
00:01:02 Liam Carter: and security — we need to know options for private deploy (VPC) and KMS integration for keys, plus audit logs for regulatory reasons.
00:01:11 Jordan Li: absolutely — we'll walk the options later in the call. For now, demo the catalog: filters you see in console: model size, architecture family, quantization profile, verified perf. For open models we tag whether there's a Redwood-verified latency profile on standard sequence lengths.
00:01:31 00:01:35 Zoe Chen: (screen share) starting with catalog, here's a quick search for 'instruction-tuned, Llama-like' — you can add a filter for tokenization quirks, which matters for your clinical tokens.
00:01:50 Sofia Rueda: quick question, do you include any domain-specific fine-tuned models or is it generic open models only?
00:01:57 Jordan Li: For the catalog demo today we're showing base open models and a few community-tuned variants. For clinical we'll often recommend you run a short fine-tune or RLHF stage; Redwood doesn't host training but we show compatibility and expected perf deltas in the bench notes.
00:02:15 Evan Brooks: Got it. show us how you narrow to a handful.
00:02:20 Zoe Chen: use the 'goal-oriented' filters — set 'summarization' + 'high-fidelity' + sequence length 1k-2k — catalog returns a set: Falcon-7B-instr (quant 4-bit), Llama 2-13B-chat (q4m), Mistral-7B, and a couple of Llamav3 community variants. It also surfaces an estimate: median 99th latency on A100 for 1k seq at batch=1. Those are bench-sourced numbers.
00:02:44 Maya Singh: how reliable are those median numbers? Our distribution is heavy tailed, occasional long documents up to 2.5K tokens.
00:02:52 Jordan Li: Good call — catalog numbers are a starting point, they're measured on standard traces. For tail latency and your 2.5K requests we'd run a targeted bench using your traces to create a realistic profile. We also flag kernel mapping: some models run on faster kernels at 2K seq because of fused attention kernels.
00:03:12 Liam Carter: about kernel mapping, are these automatic? like does Redwood pick the kernel at runtime?
00:03:18 Zoe Chen: yes, the runtime selects kernel paths based on model architecture, sequence length and quantization. The compatibility matrix shows which kernels were benchmarked (e.g., fused-attn, flash-attn, cuda-optimized) and on which HW.
00:03:30 00:03:35 Jordan Li: (note) a lot of customers miss that quant profile + sequence length combo can flip winner models. A 7B quantized model might beat a 13B at <512 tokens but not for long summaries.
00:03:48 Evan Brooks: that's a key thing — our Product team prioritized lower cost per token, but clinicians told us they'd rather wait a bit for accuracy. So quality is first then cost.
00:03:58 Sofia Rueda: exactly, accuracy > cost for us, but we can't have >2s p95.
00:04:07 Jordan Li: Perfect — that maps to a multi-tier approach: propose candidate models tuned for quality, run bench with your traces to verify p50/p95/p99, then pick a deployment mode. We usually recommend starting hosted for speed-to-insight, then move to Dedicated or Private if you need predictable throughput or strict data controls.
00:04:24 Maya Patel: quick interjection on pricing — hosted lets you move faster but may cost more at scale; Dedicated gives predictability but requires commit. We'll send a cost model later.
00:04:33 00:04:36 Zoe Chen: back to the compatibility matrix — here's an example CSV export: columns include model, arch family, quant profile, kernel tested, hw (A100/RTX6000/H100), median latency for seq lengths 512/1024/2048, token throughput, and notes on failure modes.
00:04:54 Maya Singh: Do you also annotate tokenization mismatches? we saw weird token splits when we tried Llama2 on some clinical abbreviations.
00:05:02 Jordan Li: yes we include a 'tokenization caveats' column that flags known mismatches; also the bench template includes a quick tokenization diagnostic you can run locally.
00:05:12 Evan Brooks: ok show an example decision path — like how you'd pick between Falcon-7B and Llama2-13B for us.
00:05:18 Zoe Chen: Sure — example: for 1k-1.2k summaries, Llama2-13B-chat (q4m) shows higher quality on our rouge/chrF checks but has ~1.6x latency vs Falcon-7B-unmerged at same quant on A100. But Llama2's quant profile offers better fidelity after calibration. So tradeoff: if you need sub-1s median, go Falcon; if you need strict fidelity for edge cases, Llama2 or a tuned 13B variant.
00:05:48 Liam Carter: on hardware, we're evaluating G4dn-like instances vs A100 — how big is the perf delta typically?
00:05:55 Jordan Li: substantial. A100/H100 show much better throughput for long sequences. The matrix shows normalized perf vs A100; expect 2-4x slower on GPU optimized for inference like G4dn for large seqs. We can propose a hardware map for your predicted traffic.
00:06:12 Sofia Rueda: any notes on caching? clinicians sometimes ask for iterative edits to the same note, so prefix caching could help.
00:06:19 Zoe Chen: yes, we demoed prefix/KV caching in the Optimize product — if you have repeated prefixes (patient metadata) caching can reduce token work significantly and improve p95. We'll recommend cache policies during the POC.
00:06:29 Maya Singh: how do you handle sensitive PHI with hosted? are tokens logged?
00:06:34 Maya Patel: Redwood hosted offers non-persistent logs option and we can integrate customer-managed KMS for key control. For strict PHI requirements, Private deployment in VPC or on-prem is the normal route — that gives you full control over logs and storage. We'll attach our security docs.
00:06:51 Evan Brooks: okay good. Back to benching — will the bench template let us run quality tests (e.g., clinical-specific metrics)?
00:06:58 Jordan Li: Yes, the bench template includes slots for custom evals — you can drop in your rouge/precision metrics and we run-quality checks alongside latency runs. We also provide a reproducible harness so you can re-run with different seeds.
00:07:12 00:07:18 Zoe Chen: (screen) here's a quick bench result example: Falcon-7B quant4-bit — median 0.9s at 1k seq on A100, p95 1.7s. Llama2-13B q4m — median 1.5s, p95 2.6s. Quality delta shows Llama2 with +3.2% on the clinical F1 metric for our sample bench.
00:07:36 Maya Singh: ok those numbers make sense. The p95 for Llama2 is a bit worrying. Could quant tuning or kernel choice reduce that?
00:07:44 Jordan Li: sometimes yes — using a mixed precision fallback or a different kernel reduces p95 by up to 20% in some workloads. But often the model size itself drives working set and KV cache memory pressure which affects tails. That's why we recommended targeted runs.
00:07:58 Evan Brooks: are there built-in fallbacks to smaller models if latency SLO is missed?
00:08:03 Zoe Chen: yes — Redwood routing policies can fallback from a primary model to a cheaper variant or an accelerated quant profile when latency thresholds are violated. You can configure percent-based rollouts and automatic fallback.
00:08:13 Sofia Rueda: does fallback change output quality abruptly? clinicians will notice.
00:08:18 Jordan Li: it can. We recommend A/B or canary rollouts and a quality monitor hook tied to a set of test prompts; Redwood Optimize can alert on regressions. For safety-critical output we usually avoid silent fallback without alerts.
00:08:32 Maya Patel: quick commercial note — fallback to cheaper models can save cost but risks quality. We'll include cost delta scenarios in the spreadsheet.
00:08:40 00:08:44 Evan Brooks: switching gears — we need to understand the private deployment timeline. If we sign for Private, how long to stand up?
00:08:50 Jordan Li: Depends on network and security review. Typical VPC deployment is 4-6 weeks if you use our private control plane; fully on-prem air-gapped setups can be 8-12 weeks. That includes KMS integration and audit log hookup. We'll put a timeline in the POC scoping doc.
00:09:06 Liam Carter: for dedicated capacity — how predictable is throughput for steady state? what are autoscale knobs?
00:09:12 Zoe Chen: Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools with configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity; throughput guarantees are part of the SLA. You can set headroom levels and burst windows. We can map your traffic to expected instance types.
00:09:25 Maya Singh: one more technical: for long-doc summarization we often keep full KV across multiple turns, so memory management becomes critical. How do you surface KV usage?
00:09:33 Jordan Li: the runtime exposes token-level memory telemetry: per-request KV size, cache hit rates, and recommended segmentation policy. That data feeds back into the Optimize recommendations for quantization and batch sizing.
00:09:46 Evan Brooks: this is all helpful. let's talk about next steps quickly.
00:09:50 Maya Patel: proposed next steps: send bench template and catalog export, Redwood to run a quick 'sanity bench' on one or two models with sample traces, schedule POC scoping for next week. Anything else?
00:10:02 Evan Brooks: please include a simple decision matrix example for quality vs cost — product would like that.
00:10:07 Zoe Chen: will do. Also we'll include a short how-to for tokenization checks and a runbook for running local benches.
00:10:15 Sofia Rueda: and security docs.
00:10:17 Maya Patel: yes security docs and SOC2 summary will be included.
00:10:21 00:10:25 Jordan Li: Action items recap: Maya (Redwood) sends bench template + pricing model, Jordan prepares latency/cost estimates for listed models, Cobalt shares traces and SLOs. We'll confirm POC scoping time in the calendar.
00:10:38 Evan Brooks: sounds good. Thanks everyone.
00:10:40 Maya Patel: thanks — we'll follow up with the materials.
